# BGRA and DDS Compatibility Migration Procedure

`UndertaleModLib/Models/UndertaleSprite.cs` remains the reference point for reviewing this investigation. The previous version described the DDS wrapper too much like a final solution. After review, we can only confirm that the wrapped result needs to be assessed separately; a first pass without errors does not establish that it can be processed again.

The migration sequence used at the time was as follows.

1. First, retain the original BGRA image for comparison. Do not infer the original pixel state from an already wrapped result.
2. After creating the DDS wrapper, record the output of the first pass. To verify the round trip, process that output again rather than reuse the assessment from the first pass.
3. If the second pass fails, return to the pre-wrapping image path and retain the failed object so that it is not lumped together with ordinary display issues.

```
Old assessment
Original image → DDS wrapper → Can continue processing

Separate records after review
Original image → DDS wrapper → First-pass result
                         └→ Second-pass result, assessed separately
```

The two arrows in the diagram are not two export options. The upper line retains the earlier working assumption: once the wrapper was created, subsequent processing could reuse the original result. The lower line is the recording approach added after review. It requires leaving the first-pass result where it is and starting another pass separately; the second-pass result must not be written into the first-pass result field.

"Round trip" here only checks whether the wrapper result can enter another processing pass. It does not establish conclusions about all exports, rendering, or file formats. An earlier claim was that, as long as the wrapper could be created, the resulting object was no different from the original image. That statement is retained as an old assessment and can no longer be used to decide whether the migration is complete.

During review, also avoid working backward: do not first see that the DDS result is normal and then treat the original image as verified. The original object and the wrapped result support different assessments. The former is used to check whether the image was preserved before entering the wrapper; the latter is used to check whether the intermediate object can enter processing again. Both may be normal, or only the former may be normal. In the latter case, "displays normally" must not hide the problem.

The rollback scope is narrower as a result: if the second pass behaves abnormally, do not keep rewriting the original image to accommodate the wrapper. First return to retaining the original object and stop approving based on the second-pass result, then check whether the abnormality occurs before or after wrapping. If it appears only on the second pass, the original image should still be retained for comparison. If the state before wrapping can no longer be confirmed, do not attribute the problem to the DDS wrapper itself.

This update has not removed the old path, because existing investigations still start from "wrapper created successfully." When continuing from that entry point, add a second-pass record rather than expand the old assessment into a stronger compatibility commitment. Ownership of the original object and the identity of the converted object also remain unconfirmed by this review.

Still unconfirmed: byte initialization for blank images, whether conversion returns the same object, and whether these observations are consistent across images of different sizes. The latter two items should not be closed out on the basis of this wrapper review.

# BGRA and DDS Compatibility Migration Workflow

This page preserves an old migration path, not a general overview of the current image interface. The reading entry point is still `UndertaleModLib/Models/UndertaleSprite.cs`. Early investigations started here because raw BGRA images, sprite objects, and DDS wrappers appeared in the same compatibility issue; it was later discovered that presenting them as a single straight line obscured two separate checks: object identity and blank pixels.

The diagram from the previous version can still be used to locate the points of disagreement at the time:

```text
Old assessment
Raw image → DDS wrapper → Can be processed further

Separate records after review
Raw image → DDS wrapper → First result
                         └→ Result of processing again, assessed separately
```

"Can be processed further" in the diagram was once treated as a sign that migration was complete. That framing is now useful only for explaining why wrapper round-tripping was listed as a risk at the time. It does not state whether the raw image already had usable pixel content when it was created, nor whether the conversion creates a new object. The old procedure is therefore retained, but it cannot be used as a basis for skipping checks on the original object.

When working with this old path, first split the issue into two records. One covers the raw image's creation, blank pixels, and conversion; the other covers whether processing can be restarted after the DDS wrapper is generated. Even when the first result is normal, the outcome for the second record should still be recorded. If the second processing attempt does not work, the fallback is to stop using that result as grounds for approval and return to the image object from before wrapping to continue investigating; do not modify the original object to make the wrapper look acceptable.

There is one easily overlooked point in the original migration sequence: retaining the raw image is not just for comparing rendering afterward. The object before wrapping is the only place to determine whether creation and conversion changed the image's identity. Once the object has been passed to the DDS wrapper, inferring this stage from the wrapped result conflates pixel state, object identity, and the wrapper's own result into a single conclusion. Therefore, the record should first describe what happened to the original object, and only then what happened to the wrapper output.

This review fills in the previously missing creation boundary. A newly allocated GMImage(3, 2) is RawBgra, writes 24 zero bytes for blank pixels, and ConvertToRawBgra returns the same object when it is already raw BGRA.

This fact changes the original order of checks. A blank image does not acquire its pixel state only after DDS wrapping; it should be treated as raw BGRA from the moment it is created. A blank object measuring 3×2 has defined pixel content consisting of zero-valued bytes and cannot simply be treated as an unfilled placeholder object. For an object that is already raw BGRA, conversion is not an opportunity to replace the object, either. Therefore, round-trip records need to retain observations of whether the same object continues to be used, rather than merely saying "conversion succeeded".

The old migration instructions recommended generating the wrapper first, then deciding whether to retain the original object. That recommendation no longer applies: it makes it easy for the wrapper result to mask blank pixels and object identity. The raw image state should now be confirmed first, then the DDS wrapper generated; after wrapping is complete, separately test whether that result can be processed again. The two observations address different questions and cannot cancel each other out.

This does not make the DDS wrapper an irrelevant step. For the old path, it remains an intermediate object whose result must be recorded. The first result after wrapping can show that this step was completed, but does not automatically show that its output can serve as input to the next processing pass. Only by restarting processing from that output can a record for the "wrapper round trip" side be obtained. If the second processing attempt does not work, stop at the failure after the wrapper result rather than going back to modify the already-verified raw BGRA object.

The retained fallback paths are as follows:

- If the raw image state does not match expectations, stop at creation and conversion and do not proceed to assess the wrapper round trip. In this case, the first result from DDS should not be used in place of a record of blank pixels or object identity.
- If the raw state matches expectations but the DDS result cannot be processed again, retain the original object and the first result, and revoke the old assumption that "the wrapper can be processed further". Continue investigating the issue based on the wrapped object; do not attribute it to a failure to create the raw image successfully.
- If the first wrapping result was not retained, even if the display can be reproduced later, it cannot be retroactively recorded as a pass for that original round trip. A new round of separate records can be made, but objects from the new round should not be mixed into the old migration results.
- Only when results have been recorded for both sides should this example be used as a reference for this old migration path; it still does not represent other sizes or other DDS variants.

The question mark over "different sizes" is retained here because the current creation boundary covers only blank images of 3×2. This is enough to correct the old claim that blank pixels were left entirely for the wrapper to handle, but it cannot provide the same record for other sizes. DDS variants stop at the same point as well: this page has no material that would generalize the result of one particular wrapper round trip into a shared result for all variants.

One related issue has not yet been split off from this page: the shortest real example for DDS Wrapper Round Trip should be selected from existing regression tests, and it should be confirmed whether the first result can still be processed again. No sample is invented here, nor is correct rendering treated as a substitute result. The selected example should allow the original object before wrapping, the first wrapping result, and the second processing result all to be retained; otherwise, it can only demonstrate one part and cannot support a judgment about the entire migration path.

Therefore, this record is still useful for explaining why the old path is split into two stages and which stage to fall back to when something goes wrong. It is no longer suitable for supporting the judgment that "successful wrapping means migration is complete". The old diagram and wording are retained so that people arriving through the old investigation entry point can see that what was missed at the time was the creation boundary, rather than mistakenly thinking that the DDS wrapper itself had already been proven to be problem-free.

# Legacy room tile compression experiment notes

Legacy room tile compression and Animation Curve Subobject Counts are in the same note this time because both are held up by legacy-data checks for the compatibility train: the former needs confirmation that the read pointer does not go past the room record, and the latter needs confirmation that the counting entry point does not treat the container itself as a child object. Start the room-side investigation around `UndertaleModLib/Models/UndertaleRoom.cs`. This is a useful place to trace back from because the legacy room objects and the read process are within the same model scope; other branches of the compression format were not examined this time. First save the reader position before the call, then read one complete legacy tile row, and then check only whether the resulting offset is at the end of that record. If the offset is wrong, first record the row contents and remaining bytes; don't immediately attribute anomalies in subsequent fields to the tile object.

The sample we can pin down in this round is:

> The legacy 2024.2 compressed room-tile row encodes four values of 9 as 83 09 00 00 00, round-trips through ReadCompressedTileData, and leaves the reader exactly at the record end.

This sample is the baseline for room compression checks and should not be replaced with a normal uncompressed row. In particular, keep the end-of-record position check alongside the round-trip bytes: seeing four values read out does not establish that subsequent room fields weren't consumed prematurely. If the end position is off, first recheck the incoming reader position; without the pre-read state of the same record, the returned tile values alone are of no use for debugging.

For animation curves, only the entry point and result are being recorded side by side at this stage. What needs to be counted is the child objects held by the curves, not the curve collection, room resources, or temporary lists used during serialization. There aren't enough samples to set fixed rules for the results with empty curves, multiple curves, and nested references, so the count field is left blank. Next time, change only the number of curve child objects, keep the other room contents from the same input, and then compare with the object count after reading is complete.

These two checks can run in the same compatibility review, but failures must be recorded separately. A tile-row failure should include the raw bytes and reader position; a curve-count failure should include the object hierarchy and the actual count obtained. Combining them into a single "legacy resource read failure" would obscure whether the problem lies in byte boundaries or object ownership.

To add: a minimal animation-curve input and child-object counts that can be compared before and after reading.

# Decision on Boolean Checks and LTS Requirements

In the 2024.6 compatibility train, Boolean Equivalence Check and LTS Branch Version Status were grouped into the same batch of compatibility issues, but they should not be recorded as a single check result. For the former, go back to the call sites that still use that check; for the latter, identify specific branches and example versions.

Combining them would mistake version status for a side effect of expression behavior. Leaving them combined would mean later investigations still start from the issue name, with no way to tell whether to look for the caller first or add version tests first. The two tracks can appear in the same compatibility review, but one case cannot be used to draw a conclusion about the other.

For Boolean Equivalence Check, the record should include the caller, the version in use, the entry point into the check, and the result at the time. For LTS Branch Version Status, repository tests should be added based on user-reported examples; if any fail, retain the failure text or output bytes.

versions.body:
# Decision on Boolean Checks and LTS Requirements

This record began with a classification dispute in the 2024.6 compatibility train. Boolean Equivalence Check and LTS Branch Version Status appeared in the same batch of regression questions, and the old records directed readers toward the compiler area in both cases, making it easy to treat them as a single compatibility conclusion awaiting confirmation. The decision in the initial draft was not to label a particular version, but first to separate the issues by what they address.

This addendum retains the choices made in the initial draft and adds the entry points later found for each workstream during actual verification. Both matters can still emerge from the same round of regression review, but the record must make it clear to future readers: caller review answers which entry point and version produced which result for a check; version-specific example testing answers whether the user-reported LTS branch status has been captured in inspectable material in the repository.

## Choices Retained from the Initial Draft

Three options were initially proposed.

The first was to treat LTS Branch Version Status as an outcome of Boolean Equivalence Check. On the surface, the advantage was having only one regression item to maintain: find where the check is used, then record the observed behavior on the same line. That was also the problem. A call site can establish the version, entry point, and current result at that site, but it cannot establish a conclusion about the branch status in the user's report. If a separate test later needs to be added for the version-specific example, the merged item gives no indication of what needs to be added.

The second was to retain two subjects of inspection side by side in the compatibility train's regression review. Material for Boolean Equivalence Check would be organized by caller; material for LTS Branch Version Status would be organized by version-specific example. They can be reviewed at the same time and appear in the same release material, but neither side's results can be inferred from the other's.

The third was to defer the split and wait for a new failure sample before deciding. This approach avoids making overly broad statements when material is scarce, but it provides no stable direction for verifying the compatibility questions that have already arisen. The next time someone sees only "boolean" or "LTS", they would still have to work backward from the old issue names to guess which route to take.

The second option was chosen. This decision addresses only the boundaries of recordkeeping and verification, and does not declare in advance that a particular caller, a particular LTS branch, or the entire train is compatible. At the time, the initial draft had not preserved enough call results, nor a version-specific failure sample that could be recounted here, so it did not present material still to be added as a conclusion.

## What Each Type of Material Answers

Material for Boolean Equivalence Check starts with the caller. At a minimum, a review should identify the call site still using the check, its actual version, the entry point used for the check, and the result obtained at the time. Merely writing "Boolean Equivalence Check is used here" is not enough for later comparison: the same name may appear at different entry points, and retaining only the name loses the version and context.

Material for LTS Branch Version Status starts with the version-specific example referenced in the user's report. The example should be added as a repository test; if failures remain, retain the failure text or output bytes alongside the test material. The focus here is the example's status once it is included in testing, not covering all versions with a blanket "LTS works fine". The report itself provides a starting point for investigation, while the test gives subsequent reviews something to continue examining.

The minimum required records differ between the two sides. On the caller side, the focus is the entry point and result, while on the version-specific example side, it is the branch status and test material. Recording both as "covered" loses this distinction; treating a sample from either side as proof for the other also makes the failure behavior impossible to classify.

The initial draft once used a broader working formulation: finding a caller still using Boolean Equivalence Check would suffice to characterize this regression item. That statement is suitable only as a starting point for finding samples, and was not retained as a sufficient basis for judgment. A caller can provide useful actual results, but those still describe only its own location, version, and entry point.

Likewise, LTS status cannot be treated as a release marker following a boolean check. The branch's version status needs to go into testing with the version-specific example, rather than being inferred incidentally from the result of evaluating an expression. The initial draft had no material supporting that inference, so this broad formulation was not extended further.

## Reading Entry Point for Parser.cs

UndertaleModLib/Compiler/Parser.cs is retained in this record because the old investigation directed readers here based on issue names and call names. It is suitable as a local starting point for reviewing historical behavior: first continue reading through references related to the file, then write what is found back into the specific call sample.

This location does not serve as the test checklist for LTS Branch Version Status, nor does it automatically become the implementation home for the two requirements. The old investigation already provided a file from which to start reading, while the current review must put what is learned back under the correct record subject. For Boolean Equivalence Check, the results should go back to the caller entry; for LTS examples, the results should go back to the corresponding test material.

The repository index lists this path as an existing C# module for code reading and checking historical behavior. When revisiting old references, use internal/undertale-core's v_prev as the entry point for the corresponding version. The path is retained so the starting point of the old investigation is not lost, not to make the filename a substitute for a compatibility judgment.

## Two Later Verification Entry Points

UMT-207 recorded a caller_walkthrough. It brought "Boolean Equivalence Check" back from a generic issue name to a caller check: find the call site still using the check, then verify its actual version, entry point, and current result. This is consistent with the initial draft's decision to separate the two, and also shows why adding samples later should not amount to adding only the name of a check.

The local description for UMT-218 retained another workstream: add repository tests based on the user-reported LTS Branch Version Status examples, and retain the current failure text or output bytes. The card subsequently underwent security_triaged, and was then recorded as work_started (To Do → In Progress). These actions show that the relevant material is being worked on, not that the tests have passed or that a final conclusion has been reached on the branch status.

The two cards serve different purposes on this page. UMT-207 takes readers back to the callers awaiting verification; UMT-218 takes readers back to the version-specific example tests that still need to be added. Both belong to this batch of compatibility work, but the processing actions on the cards are not recast as technical conclusions here.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Side-by-Side Registration" as Registered
    state "Caller Verification" as Caller
    state "Add Version-Specific Examples to Tests" as LtsCase
    state "Regression Review" as Review

    [*] --> Registered
    Registered --> Caller: Boolean Equivalence Check
    Registered --> LtsCase: LTS Branch Version Status
    Caller --> Review
    LtsCase --> Review
    Review --> [*]
```

The merge point in the diagram only indicates that material from both workstreams can enter regression review together, not that they have already reached the same conclusion before merging. Caller results still belong in caller records, and version-specific example results still belong in test records. With this arrangement, readers starting from a regression item can find two distinct lines of follow-up inquiry instead of seeing only a vague compatibility status.

## Consolidation Approaches Not Adopted

Parser.cs was not made the sole checkpoint under a unified entry point. Doing so would make it seem that caller review can start from only one file, and would also wrongly place LTS test material in the discussion of the compilation path. The fact that the old investigation pointed to this file is worth preserving, but it can answer only where to start reading, not where each piece of material belongs.

No single shared pass/fail conclusion was used to combine the two workstreams either. The current result for Boolean Equivalence Check may come from a particular call site; the status of a LTS example may come from a repository test. The two observe different subjects, so even if neither shows an anomaly in a given review, their respective results can only be recorded separately.

The option of deferring the split was not reinstated either. There is now an entry point for caller review, as well as a clear direction for adding LTS examples as tests. Continuing to keep them in one undivided item awaiting investigation would only leave new material without a fixed place.

This decision also does not cover decompiler compatibility or Local Declaration Rendering State. That set of interface review materials is maintained in DOC-16; this page retains only the history of Boolean Equivalence Check and LTS Branch Version Status, to avoid presenting this batch of work as one large topic without boundaries.

## Current Recordkeeping Method

1. When adding a Boolean Equivalence Check sample, first clearly record the caller, actual version, entry point, and current result. If only a name or issue name is found, retain it as a reading lead for now, rather than listing it as a regression result.

2. When adding material for LTS Branch Version Status, first identify which user-reported version-specific example it corresponds to, then add it to the repository tests. The failure text or output bytes should be saved together with the example, not reduced to a summary of "failed" in the rollup.

3. During regression review, the two workstreams appear side by side. The summary may state which material was examined in this round, but must not use a single call sample to draw a conclusion about version status, nor a single version test to draw a conclusion about all call sites.

4. When revisiting the old reading paths, continue searching from the related references in UndertaleModLib/Compiler/Parser.cs and v_prev. Archive the findings separately under callers or version tests, rather than duplicating them in a third type of mixed entry.

5. Cards serve only as navigation to the material. UMT-207 corresponds to caller verification, and UMT-218 corresponds to LTS example testing; as further processing records are added to the cards, whether this decision needs to change depends on whether those records change the recordkeeping boundaries for the two workstreams, not on the card status itself.

What is still missing is not a more complete overview, but concrete samples. Actual caller-side results have not yet been saved on this page; complete failure text or output bytes have not been saved on this page for the LTS side either. If a behavior later appears that involves both a call entry point and version status, retain a call sample and a version test separately, then determine whether the two pieces of material point to the same actual relationship.

At present, no third "Combined Boolean and LTS" category is being added. Only when both caller records and version-specific example tests clearly point to the same actual relationship is there reason to describe them as sharing a common cause; until then, keeping them side by side is more faithful to the available material than merging them.

# Decompiler Compatibility Adjustment Plan

This page continued to be used as a reference for the compatibility issue involving 2024.6, but it records an interface trial rather than a finalized decompiler specification. The review entry point is still `UndertaleModLib/Decompiler/Decompiler.cs`. This is where local declarations and their adjacent objects can first be seen; early discussions grouped both issues around this area, which avoided the initial search but also made the "shared state" judgment below seem more certain than it actually was.

> Initial draft handling: Split Decompiler Compatibility and Local Declaration Rendering State shared a single context entry point. After the split, handling was still determined by the same context; local declarations also obtained their rendering state from it. This kept the change surface small, and troubleshooting required comparing only one output.
>
> The initial draft retained a rollback point: if repeated processing and local-declaration rendering produced results pointing in different directions, they would no longer be treated as the same state issue.

The paragraph above was not deleted. It explains why merging was favored at the time: both issues appeared in the compatibility train, and both names pointed to decompiler output. It was not an interface conclusion. The later review found no basis for directly inferring "the same rendering state" from "near the same file," so this round keeps the trial split rather than adding a larger shared switch.

First, distinguish the two observation points:

- **Split Decompiler Compatibility** is concerned with whether the content or diagnostics for the same object remain stable after initial and repeated processing. What must be retained here is the difference between the two processing passes, rather than prescribing in advance what a particular kind of text must look like.
- **Local Declaration Rendering State** is concerned with the actual output the tool produces after source code that directly triggers Local Declaration Rendering State goes through the existing entry point. It can be part of the same review round as the first observation, but the input, output, and assessment are stored separately.

This distinction also explains why "local declarations" are not treated as a sub-claim of split compatibility. The former may show up as source rendering; the latter may show up as changes in content or diagnostics before and after processing. Even if both ultimately need to touch `Decompiler.cs`, one observation must not vouch for the other during the trial.

## Two Remaining Candidates

**Candidate A: Continue sharing the context entry point.**

The benefit is that the changes stay localized. If all related calls originally depended on the same context, the local-declaration state and the compatibility branch for split processing could be adjusted together. This is the direction the initial draft took.

The trade-off is that when something fails, it is difficult to tell where the change came from. A change in local-declaration output could be mistakenly recorded as a side effect of split compatibility; unstable diagnostics from repeated processing could likewise be incorrectly attributed to rendering state. This direction is worth continuing only if two sets of independent samples actually show the same state boundary.

**Candidate B: Keep the existing entry point; add separate observations and make minimal adjustments.**

This does not presuppose shared fields on the two sides, nor put the compatibility determination into the declaration-rendering path. Split processing compares only the first and second runs; local declarations record only the direct input and actual output. When a change is needed, try it first within each local boundary, rather than expanding the change in the name of "interface unification."

This round adopts B as the trial order. It does not claim that there will ultimately be two long-lived interfaces; it simply gives the two failure modes separate samples first. Once the samples show a common state source, discuss whether to merge. This decision is more conservative than the initial draft, and it also means a tidy unified entry point will not be available in the short term.

## Materials to Retain

The investigation item for UMT-208 requires initial and repeat processing to be run separately, with a record of whether the content or diagnostics are stable. During review, retain the two results side by side; if a difference appears only on the second run, label it first as a repeated-processing boundary, and do not immediately add local declarations to the reproduction conditions.

UMT-211 in turn requires a source snippet that directly triggers Local Declaration Rendering State, as well as the actual output after that input goes through the existing entry point. Here, "directly" matters: the sample should not depend on intermediate results already changed by split processing. If the behavior can only be seen on a mixed path, record the mixed path as such; do not pass it off as a standalone reproduction of local declarations.

The caller's StringBuilder insertion remains a separate boundary, handled under DOC-17. It may affect the final concatenated text, but it should not be used to prove state ownership inside `Decompiler.cs`. Conversely, if the local-declaration sample appears anomalous only after caller insertion, record that condition in the sample first rather than forcing the issue into this proposal.

## Signals to Stop

Candidate B still must not be presented as a completed design in any of the following cases:

- The difference between initial and repeated processing cannot be reproduced consistently, or only diagnostic text remains, with no content to compare;
- The local-declaration input cannot be saved outside the mixed path, making it impossible to determine whether it is actually an independent rendering state;
- Both sample sets point to Caller StringBuilder Insertion, while `Decompiler.cs` only passes through the output chain;
- To make the sample pass, one must first assume an unconfirmed shared context.

The first three cases should remain at the recording level; do not add an interface. The fourth directly rolls back the old approach of "merge first, validate later." Rolling back only restores the separation of the issues; it does not require deleting the old paragraph. The old paragraph still explains why this page initially put the two names together.

The scope confirmation for UMT-208 was completed later, but that action did not replace the samples. What is still missing is: exactly what content repeated processing compares, what output the local-declaration sample actually leaves under the existing entry point, and whether the two sides will converge on the same local state. Only after these materials are complete will the shared-entry-point draft on this page be worth reopening.

# Decision record for the buffer release boundary

This record was initially treated as a very narrowly scoped window-side compatibility item: the earlier investigation left behind the issue name "Buffer release Boundaries" and set the lookup location to `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs`. People continued to use that link later, so it was not deleted. It could lead people to the file examined at the time, but it did not also preserve the release call chain, object ownership, or reproduction conditions.

The initial draft's wording leaned toward "window-side". This was a trade-off made at the time to preserve the investigation's starting point, not confirmation of where the implementation resided. Looking back now, the useful part of the old wording is that the filename and issue name still line up; the inaccurate part is that it can easily make people think the window file already explains when release is called on the buffer, who holds the read position, and where the exception is returned from. Those details were not recorded at the time.

## The earlier decision retained

The initial draft effectively chose between two options.

- Delete this record outright and log it again once a caller is identified.
- Temporarily retain the window file as the first stop and continue calling the issue a window-side boundary.

The second option was chosen at the time. The earlier investigation had already reached this file through the issue name and call name; if this location were also removed, later readers would have to start over from the vague term "release". The decision to retain it was not made because the window layer had been proven responsible, but because the existing trail used to locate it should not be lost.

That decision also implied a working sequence that later needed correcting: first look for a sufficient explanation in the window file, then decide whether to trace the caller. This sequence mistook "a file that can be opened" for "a question that can be answered". Subsequent review did not support equating the two, so the old conclusion is retained here unchanged, but no longer serves as grounds for closing the issue.

> Previous position: treat Buffer release Boundaries as a window-side issue for now; `MainWindow.xaml.cs` is the starting point for investigation.
>
> Correction: it is still the starting point for investigation, but is no longer regarded as the place to determine responsibility for the boundary.

## The snippets actually left in the file

What can currently be pinpointed reliably is a few local sections of this file. At the beginning of the file, line 55 declares `namespace UndertaleModTool`. This places it within the application's window namespace, but the declaration itself does not provide the semantics of release.

Later in the window code, there is resource access:

```csharp
var resources = Application.Current.Resources;
```

This snippet is at line 265. Nearby, line 278 reads:

```csharp
const long SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED = 0x08000000;
```

Further down, line 332 opens a class key in the user registry:

```csharp
var HKCU_Classes = Registry.CurrentUser.OpenSubKey(@"Software\Classes", true);
```

These snippets show that the old starting point did not arbitrarily point to a nonexistent file: this really is window code, and it contains local operations for resources, association changes, and registry handling. But they do not form a code path for "reading after buffer release". Connecting them into such a path was an overinterpretation left by the initial draft.

Other nearby binding names in the same file include `UndertaleModTool`, `resources`, `long`, `HKCU_Classes`, `UndertaleModTool_app`, `ext`, and `args`. Some of these names are enough to help continue looking within the file for window initialization or association settings; they should not be used as substitutes for a specific caller. In particular, `ext` and `args` are merely binding names that can be located in this snapshot, and the old record did not describe their relationship to the buffer object.

The role of the file location in this decision should therefore be narrowed to a "lookup anchor". It preserves the direction taken by the earlier investigation and limits further reading to a local section that can be checked, rather than presenting a series of nonadjacent pieces of window code as a release implementation.

## Later notes

In UMT-215, the verification item left later was very specific: find a caller still using "Buffer release Boundaries" and verify its actual version, entry point, and current result. This verification item changed the focus of this record. The original question was "whether the window file is still worth examining", and it later became "which caller can provide the three facts needed to assess the boundary".

The card also recorded that a design comparison was performed, but the comparison's content was not developed here into a new conclusion about the mechanism. What can be confirmed is that the earlier window-file finding did not directly lead to marking the issue as resolved at the time. A subsequent note also preserved the judgment made then:

> Don't close this one yet, for this section of Adaptive Binary Read Boundaries, Buffer release Boundaries still has one unconfirmed point, update it when the next fact comes in.

This sentence did not identify the specific call at the unconfirmed point, nor did it provide a runtime result. Its value lies in explicitly rejecting the reasoning that "the file has been found, so the issue is over". The initial draft only left the starting point for the first half; the later note documented the stopping point for the second half.

## Approach after comparing the options again

During review, the available approaches can be distinguished more clearly without inventing facts to fill gaps in the old record.

The first approach is to continue treating the window file as the location responsible. The advantage is a short path, with no change to the old investigation name; the cost is that readers can easily infer a buffer chain that does not exist in the record from `Application.Current.Resources`, association-change constants, or registry access. This approach carries forward the convenience of the initial draft, but magnifies the part of it that lacked evidence.

The second approach is to delete all window-side references and leave only "waiting for a caller". This avoids misleading people with the old wording, but also loses the only existing file navigation. For people who still look back using the historical issue name, this is worse than retaining a starting point with a correction.

The third approach is to retain the old label and file location while downgrading them from attribution conclusions to search clues; the material actually used to assess the release boundary must come from a caller still using that boundary. The third approach was adopted after review.

This is not shifting the problem elsewhere. The window file should still be opened first, because the earlier investigation has already left visible traces here; but the goal of reading it has changed. All that is needed now is to check whether it can point further to a specific call, rather than explain the buffer's entire lifecycle here. If the file does not contain this connection, the next step is not to keep expanding window-side speculation, but to look for the caller's version, entry point, and current result as specified in the verification item.

## Revised decision

From now on, this record retains two levels and no longer conflates them.

1. "Window-side" is the old investigation label. It describes where the search historically began, not responsibility for the implementation.
2. `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs` is the file anchor that can currently be revisited. Lines 55, 265, 278, and 332 provide explicit reading locations, but do not provide the full call relationships for release.
3. Whether Buffer release Boundaries has a compatibility anomaly depends on the caller still using that boundary and its actual version, entry point, and current result. If any one of these is missing, the status must remain unconfirmed.

This revision also explains why the old file location is not being replaced with another guessed module name. The input contains no second confirmed call entry point; switching to a path that looks more like a binary-reading implementation would only create a new break in the historical trail. The old starting point can be retained, provided readers can see that it no longer carries responsibility for attribution.

The following state diagram describes only the reading sequence permitted by this record, not the program's runtime state:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> OldIssueName
    OldIssueName --> MainWindowLocation
    MainWindowLocation --> CallerPendingVerification
    CallerPendingVerification --> RetainUMT_215
```

The `MainWindowLocation` in the diagram is not a success state. It indicates that the historical record can still lead a review to the same file; there is no transition from here to "CallerPendingVerification" that the existing snippets can fill in. `RetainUMT_215` also does not mean treating the card as an implementation description, but rather keeping the three facts from the actual environment that have not yet been obtained on the original verification item.

## The old starting point that still applies

Anyone looking back from "Buffer release Boundaries" can still open `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs` first. First check whether a clear clue to a call can be found near window-related bindings, resource access, association changes, or registry handling; if not, these adjacent snippets should not be treated as buffer evidence. The value left by the old record ends here.

If a candidate caller is found, its actual version, the entry point through which the call is reached, and the current result need to be recorded together. Only then can two completely different situations be distinguished: the window file was merely searched in the past, or the window path really is still involved in triggering the issue. The initial draft did not have enough material to make this distinction, and the later notes did not provide the answer on its behalf.

## The remaining item not split out

"Adaptive Binary Read Boundaries" appears next to this issue in the later notes, but the two are not merged here. They may share the context of an investigation, or they may simply be two unconfirmed boundaries from the same round; the existing record is insufficient to tell. Buffer release Boundaries continues to retain its own old label, file anchor, and pending caller verification item.

This page therefore remains a decision record from an earlier point in time, not new operating instructions. It corrects the scope of the window-side attribution, but does not claim that the caller's version, entry point, or current result has been obtained.

# Texture Pool and Tile Alignment Plan

2024.6 compatibility train's interface review initially put two issues into the same record: Embedded Texture Pool Count, and 2024.4 Tile Alignment. At present, there is only one entry-point lead: `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs`. The file shows `namespace UndertaleModTool`, `var resources = Application.Current.Resources;`, `const long SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED = 0x08000000;`, and a registry-read binding, but these locations still aren't enough to establish implementation ownership for the two issues.

The preliminary plan is to gather evidence in two passes, without combining the two results into a single pass condition. The first is to find the actual call to Embedded Texture Pool Count, and save the input used by the call and the tool's externally visible result. The second is to trigger 2024.4 Tile Alignment directly from the existing entry point, retaining the input and actual output. This first separates "what the caller passed" from "what the entry point produced," then determines whether the interface needs adjustment.

There are two candidate approaches: trace back through the caller, which shows where the count and alignment parameters come from; or run a minimal reproduction through the entry point, which is easy to repeat but may bypass the real caller. Neither will be selected as the sole approach yet. # Texture Pool and Tile Alignment Plan

This proposal still retains the two issues, but withdraws one premise from the previous version: Embedded Texture Pool Count and 2024.4 Tile Alignment cannot be treated as the same interface issue merely because both investigations can start from the same place. The former needs the real call behind a report, the input fields, and the result seen by the user; the latter needs source code, input, and the tool's actual output that can trigger the old-version alignment behavior. Each route is missing some material, and the gaps are different.

The existing source-code locations are still useful; their purpose just needs to be narrowed. `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs` is located at `namespace UndertaleModTool`, and the visible local points include `var resources = Application.Current.Resources;`, `const long SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED = 0x08000000;`, and `var HKCU_Classes = Registry.CurrentUser.OpenSubKey(@"Software\\Classes", true);`. These points show that this can serve as an investigation entry point: resource binding, file association, and window-side code are indeed visible in the same file. They do not show how the embedded texture pool is counted, nor how the tiles of 2024.4 are arranged.

Therefore, the role of the path is only to bring the investigation back to a source-code site that can be inspected. It is neither a determination of ownership of the texture-pool interface nor proof of the tile-conversion logic. If the real call or triggering line found later is elsewhere, the new location should be treated as the actual evidence; it does not need to return to this file to be considered valid. The appearance of `resources`, `SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED`, or `HKCU_Classes` in the current file cannot be extrapolated into saying that texture objects, count fields, or tile data have already passed through these statements.

## This time, the two will no longer share one results table

Originally, we wanted to put the two questions into one unified record: write the input in one column, the return in one column, and whether it passed in one column. This looks convenient for comparison, but in practice it erases the differences between the two categories. The input fields for texture counting have not yet been confirmed, and filling in the table first would only force the recorder to guess field names; tile alignment instead requires saving the input before and after ordering, along with the tool output, with the focus not on whether a particular returned object is non-null. The two tasks can be included in the same review, but they cannot substitute for each other's materials.

The texture route needs at least three layers of facts to be stored separately. The first layer is the fields the caller actually passes to the interface; the second is the object or value returned by the interface; the third is the text or status the user sees in the tool. The three layers may agree, or they may not. Seeing a non-null object cannot be directly written as "there is one texture in the pool"; seeing a piece of displayed text cannot be traced back to conclude that it necessarily came from the current entry point. Only by leaving the call location, input, and displayed result side by side can we determine which layer the report's "count" actually belongs to.

The tile route does not need to wait for the texture fields. It needs a minimal fixture that can be triggered directly from an existing entry point in the source. The fixture's content, dimensions, and specific fields are not currently given in the record, so a sample cannot be invented in advance just to meet the schedule. When it can be triggered, preserve the input's original order and the ordering actually produced by the tool; when it cannot, record it as not triggered. If the tool output differs from expectations, the output itself should be retained, rather than rewritten in the record as "already aligned" or "already fixed".

When the two routes run at the same time, their results still cannot be merged into one conclusion. Missing texture fields should not obscure the output already obtained from the tile sample; differences in tile ordering also cannot be attributed to the counting interface. The review should look not at whether there was one overall success this round, but at whether each route left enough input and results for rechecking. If one route stops, the other can continue collecting its own material.

## Embedded Texture Pool Count: First find the call corresponding to the report

The local work left by UMT-217 is to find the real call for the most recent report, "Embedded Texture Pool Count", and fill in how it was called and the result seen by the user. This requirement is stricter than "finding a similar name". The issue name, call name, and implementation ownership may all differ; based only on a snippet with a similar name, it is impossible to determine whether it generated the count in the report or to confirm which fields the caller supplied.

Candidate path A prioritizes the caller. First pin down the call location corresponding to the most recent report, and transcribe only the fields actually passed by the caller and the displayed result after the call completes. The count value, whether a returned object exists, and the text appearing in the UI should be placed in separate columns; they cannot be combined into one Boolean judgment in the first-round record. The value of path A is that it can answer who consumes the interface; the cost is that if the field source remains unclear, the investigation will stop at the call boundary.

Path A does not require an immediate change to the interface. After finding the call, first confirm that the record is for the same call, rather than another branch that also obtains a texture object. The call location needs to be paired with the saved input; leaving only a line number or only a screenshot-like result cannot support the count semantics. If the call's input is incomplete, missing items should be explicitly left blank; local code for resource binding or registry reads must not be used as a substitute.

Candidate path B prioritizes the entry point. Choose a minimal input that can be reached directly from the existing tool entry point, retain the original input, interface return, and UI result separately, and then compare them with path A's call sample. It is suitable for obtaining a reproducible local sample while the fields are not yet fully confirmed, and it can also help identify cases where "the entry point is stable but the report call is different". It cannot prove that the call in the report used the same fields, and it certainly cannot independently prove the external meaning of the pool count.

The boundary of path B must be stated clearly. A minimal input producing a result at the entry point does not mean that it covers the caller involved in the real report; the absence of an anomaly in the UI does not mean that the count came from the same object. If path B's returned object differs from path A's, retain the difference first and pause before combining the two into the same interface conclusion. What needs to be added at that point is the call relationship or field source, not a declaration that one of the samples is the baseline.

Paths A and B will both produce comparable material, but they answer different questions. A answers how the consumer in the report obtains the value, while B answers what the existing entry point produces when given a minimal input. The proposal does not require them to match immediately; matching would not eliminate the need to confirm the input fields. Only when the call location, input, and result displayed by the tool can be compared item by item should we discuss whether these two observations belong to the same compatibility assessment.

## Field blocking changes the order

UMT-217 moved from To Do to In Progress in 2025-10-16, and changed to Blocked the next day. The recorded reason was that the upstream interface owner had not yet confirmed the input fields. This status change is not a progress note; it is a stopping point for the texture route. When the fields are unconfirmed, continuing to define the count semantics only puts assumptions ahead of the evidence. The previous arrangement of "write a call sample first and add the fields later" is no longer being used.

This does not mean that no part of the texture work can continue. We can continue locating the real call indicated by the report, prepare the record structure, and distinguish the returned object from the result displayed to the user; however, unknown fields cannot be defaulted to zero, an empty value, or the default configuration. Any count obtained from these defaults does not enter compatibility sign-off and cannot be used as a reason to change the interface.

After the upstream fields are confirmed, the order for resuming path A should remain disciplined: first verify that the call really corresponds to the report, then retain the fields actually passed, and finally record the result seen by the user. The call-identity check cannot be skipped just because the fields have finally appeared. Field confirmation only resolves "what the input is"; it does not automatically resolve "whether this input belongs to the call for the most recent report".

If the fields remain unconfirmed, path B can continue as a local entry-point experiment, but its conclusion must stop at entry-point behavior. It can show what a definite input produces after passing through the existing tool, but it cannot fill in the real call method for UMT-217. Upgrading B's result into a counting-interface conclusion is a shortcut that this proposal explicitly rejects.

## 2024.4 Tile Alignment: Keep the input and ordering together

The requirement from UMT-219 is more direct: use source code capable of triggering "2024.4 Tile Alignment" through the existing entry point, and save the input and the tool's actual output. The difficulty here is not whether the file can be opened by the tool, but whether the original ordering is retained after the old-version data enters the entry point. An ordinary resource-binding snippet cannot automatically become a tile sample; only source code that truly triggers the alignment behavior satisfies the starting point for this route.

The goal of the minimal fixture should be narrow: make the alignment behavior appear, rather than construct a large sample covering every resource scenario. Once the input is determined, the record needs to preserve its original order. The tool output should likewise be saved in its actual order, so that it will later be possible to see whether the ordering changed. The expected ordering is not currently frozen, so this proposal cannot write one particular ordering as the established correct answer.

If the first input does not trigger alignment, it should not be disguised as "alignment unchanged". Not triggered means that the sample is not yet an entry point to this behavior; the record should retain this status, and the search should continue for source code that reaches the behavior directly. If it has been triggered but the output is surprising, do not lump the output into the failure of texture counting. It is an observation belonging to the tile route and should be retained together with the original input.

The tile route can complete a round of material collection before the texture route because it does not depend on the input fields missing from UMT-217. This ordering does not mean that the tile issue is more important, nor that its result can replace texture validation; it only means that the current blocking conditions for the two tasks are different. If the tile result appears first, the review can first discuss whether the ordering difference needs further investigation, without waiting for the texture-field issue to end.

Putting the texture sample and tile fixture in the same run can only save preparation time; it cannot create a joint pass criterion. A joint criterion would create two kinds of misreading: blank fields in the texture route might be mistakenly written up as a tile issue, and differences in tile output might be mistakenly written up as instability in the counting interface. The record format should allow a reader to extract the input, output, and open items for either route independently.

## Changes not to submit yet

The current material is insufficient to directly change the interface semantics of Embedded Texture Pool Count. Without a real call and confirmed fields, any formulation of "what the count should be" would exceed the existing evidence. It is also insufficient to specify new ordering rules for 2024.4 Tile Alignment; UMT-219 requires saving the input and the tool's actual output, rather than presupposing a corrected result.

This means that the first deliverable of this round is two recheckable local records, not a joint change. The texture record must include at least the call location, the actual input fields, the returned object or value, and the result seen by the user. The tile record must include at least the triggerable source code, the original input order, and the tool's actual output. Empty items in both records must be retained as-is; filling them with material from the other route would create a false association.

`MainWindow.xaml.cs` can still be listed as a search entry point, but not as implementation proof in the deliverable. The resources, constants, and registry reference points currently in the file only help return to the inspectable working surface from that time. They cannot be used to determine the number of members in the texture pool, nor the old-version tile alignment result. If a more direct call or triggering line is found later, its direct location should replace this broader entry-point clue.

## This round's choice and withdrawal conditions

The choice is parallel preparation and separate interpretation. Texture counting will first wait for field confirmation while continuing to look for the real call corresponding to the report; tile alignment will first look for a triggerable minimal fixture and save the input and actual output. Neither route has been designated as a prerequisite for the other.

The corresponding judgment should be withdrawn in the following cases, rather than filled in with speculation:

- If only the issue name or a similar call name is found, but the real call corresponding to the report cannot be found, withdraw the interface judgment for texture counting.
- When the input fields have not been confirmed, do not submit a change to the count semantics, and do not interpret blank fields as zero.
- If the entry-point sample produces a return but its relationship to the real call cannot be established, retain only the entry-point observation and do not write it as the caller's result.
- If the tile input cannot be triggered through the source entry point, retain the not-triggered record and do not substitute the texture sample.
- If the tile behavior has been triggered but the input and tool output were not saved together, do not use that result to determine whether the ordering is compatible.
- Only when the material for each route can be reviewed independently should we discuss whether there is a common subsequent interface adjustment.

Only two old judgments are retained. First, `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs` is a valuable investigation entry point; second, the two questions can be tracked in the same compatibility train review. What is withdrawn is the judgment that "the same entry point is sufficient for them to share evidence and a conclusion". Having the same entry point only means that the investigation starting points are similar; it does not mean that the inputs, objects, or failure behavior are the same.

The content that remains undetermined should also stay at the end of the proposal rather than being prematurely closed out. The real call, input fields, returned object, and specific result seen by the user for Embedded Texture Pool Count still need to be filled in. The triggerable source code, minimal fixture content, and expected ordering for 2024.4 Tile Alignment are also not defined by the existing material. Until field confirmation for UMT-217 resumes, the texture route will only advance location and record preparation; UMT-219 will meanwhile continue collecting an independent sample bounded by the input and the tool's actual output.

├─ Occurs only after processing DDS

└─ Occurs after interpolation is explicitly specified

# DDS Image Interpolation Troubleshooting Tree

When image results are abnormal, first split the observed situation into two tracks: the state after DDS mipmap Consumption, and what actually gets triggered after the caller explicitly specifies image interpolation. They may occur during the same window operation, but adjacent names do not mean the processing happens in the same place. An earlier visual change also cannot substitute for confirmation of the consumption action or the interpolation setting.

Start troubleshooting with normal user calls. First record whether this operation uses DDS or another image object; then record at which stage before or after mipmap consumption the abnormal behavior is visible; finally record whether there was an action that explicitly specified interpolation. Preserve any available return values or raw diagnostics as well. If diagnostics cannot be obtained, explicitly state that no raw diagnostics are available, rather than inferring a cause from visual impressions.

```text
Start: Abnormal image results in the user path
|
+-- Can it be confirmed that the object in this operation involves a DDS payload?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Was image interpolation explicitly specified?
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   +-- Yes: Record the setting action and the user path actually taken.
|   |   |   `-- No: Retain the image object and observed behavior, but do not include them in this workflow.
|   |
|   `-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Did mipmap consumption occur in this path?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- Yes: Preserve the post-consumption state and any available return values or raw diagnostics.
|       |   `-- Unclear: Retrace the same user path; do not use the debug entry point to fill in a conclusion.
|       |
|       `-- Was interpolation also explicitly specified?
|           |
|           +-- Yes: Record DDS and interpolation separately; do not combine them into one cause.
|           `-- No: Stop after completing the trace-back for the DDS branch.
|
`-- Insufficient input or diagnostics
    `-- Stop changes and release assessments, and record the missing items.
```

## Recording Observations

A single reproduction must distinguish at least three facts: "the object has entered DDS processing", "mipmap consumption has been confirmed", and "the abnormal image result is visible". The first fact does not imply the other two; the third fact also does not allow you to infer which specific step occurred. If all that is known is that the state is abnormal after processing, it can serve as the starting point for the DDS branch, but it cannot be used to choose a recovery action.

Record explicit interpolation in the same way. Keep a record of the action that sets interpolation and the path actually reached after that action. Seeing the check run only in an example or a debug entry point shows only that this entry point can trigger the check; it cannot be recorded as coverage of normal UI operations. If the user path does not go through that check, retain the uncovered path, and do not let partial observations from DDS close it out.

When abnormal behavior involves both tracks, record it in the order it occurred, rather than replacing all observations with "the image changed". First record whether the DDS object has reached mipmap consumption, then whether interpolation was explicitly specified, and finally when the abnormal behavior became visible. If the order cannot be confirmed, retain only the shared symptoms and the missing observation points; at this stage, do not change a processing step just to try your luck.

Failure to reproduce on the normal path is also worth recording. It means the current review has not reproduced the behavior from the debug entry point in normal operations, not that the problem has disappeared. Conversely, reliably seeing the abnormal behavior in the debug entry point can only be used to continue locating references and objects, not to directly reach a compatibility judgment.

## DDS Branch

After confirming that the object involves DDS, first ask whether mipmap consumption actually occurred during this user operation. If it can be confirmed, preserve the post-consumption state, return values, or raw diagnostics; if all that is visible is a difference in the final image and there is no return information that can be retained, stop at describing the state. Do not infer from visual differences that the consumption logic has completed, and do not record such a result as an interpolation check failure.

Retracing the DDS branch should use the same user entry point. Passing the object separately into a debug entry point may help confirm that the object can be processed, but it cannot prove that normal operations in the window take the same path. When it reproduces through the normal entry point, prioritize recording the facts that occur there; when it does not reproduce through the normal entry point, record the results from that entry point and the debug entry point separately, without merging them into a single conclusion.

When no diagnostics can be obtained either before or after mipmap consumption, do not expand the scope of troubleshooting further. Simply record the object type, the known stage, and the missing output. At this point, do not switch to modifying explicit interpolation just because it is "image-related", and do not use interpolation example results to explain the DDS state.

## Explicit Image Interpolation Branch

The interpolation branch must answer whether the caller explicitly requested interpolation and whether that request reached the existing check through the user operation. The presence of some image processing in the code does not answer either question. First locate the setting action, then follow that window operation to confirm the subsequent path; when the setting appears only in an example, record it as an example result rather than extending it into coverage of the user path.

Sometimes a DDS object and an interpolation setting appear together. In that case, both records can be continued in parallel, but each must retain its own trigger conditions and diagnostics. Abnormal behavior after DDS processing does not automatically prove that the interpolation setting was read; execution of the interpolation check does not automatically prove that mipmap consumption has occurred. When either track lacks input, the other track's result cannot fill the gap.

If the interpolation setting has been established but the user path has no subsequent state that can be retained, stop at "the setting has been triggered, the result is unconfirmed". This is more accurate than marking the existing check as passed outright. User paths that have not yet been covered remain tracked under UMT-222, and this window-side trace-back is not a substitute for covering them.

## Tracing Back from the Window Side

The window-side entry point is `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs`. Known locations include line 55 for `namespace UndertaleModTool`, line 265 for `var resources = Application.Current.Resources;`, and line 278 for `const long SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED = 0x08000000;`. These locations are useful for tracing abnormal behavior back to references near normal UI operations, but resource access and association-change constants themselves are not evidence of DDS consumption or interpolation taking effect.

Further down, `var HKCU_Classes = Registry.CurrentUser.OpenSubKey(@"Software\Classes", true);` at line 332 and the adjacent application association handling may also appear in the same window context after startup. They only help establish the window environment in which the operation occurs. Until references have been followed to the image object, do not attribute the image abnormality to registry access, resource dictionaries, or file association changes.

Keep the trace-back order close to this operation: first confirm which image object the window action obtained; then confirm whether that object carries DDS data; next check whether it enters mipmap consumption; finally confirm whether there is an explicit interpolation setting. When references cease to connect to the observed operation partway through, stop there and attach the recorded observations at the break in the chain. Do not guess where the object goes in other modules just to obtain a complete chain.

The window side is not responsible for all image assessments either. It provides locations near the UI entry point, and starting here is no reason to attribute DDS processing to the window file. What is needed is a reference connecting the current operation to the object, not a declaration that merely looks related to the image issue.

## Cards and Blocking Issues

UMT-221 focuses on abnormal states after DDS mipmap Consumption. When working on it, make sure this consumption occurs through normal user calls, and preserve return values or raw diagnostics. If only the visual behavior is available locally and there are no diagnostics to preserve, report that gap back as well; do not make a release assessment based solely on the local display.

For UMT-222, use existing tests or examples to trigger Explicit Image Interpolation, and record user paths that are not yet covered back on the card. Tests or examples can confirm the trigger conditions, but they do not replace reproduction through normal window operations. Even after an example proves that the call exists, you still need to check whether the user will go through the same check.

In subsequent reviews, work related to DDS was handled under the release category; the CI queue then became blocked, and local results were not used for further judgments. A blocked queue is neither evidence that the DDS state has recovered nor evidence that the interpolation check has failed. If the same situation occurs, record only what the local results can establish and the fact that the CI queue is blocked, and stop advancing release conclusions when CI results are missing.

Do not combine the blocked CI with debug entry point results to conclude that it passed. The former lacks follow-up verification, while the latter lacks confirmation through normal calls; retain these two gaps separately. When resuming the review, first fill in the records connected to this user path, then decide which branch can proceed.

## Stop Conditions

An investigation can end at any branch point. The closing record only needs to make clear: whether it reproduced in the user path, whether DDS and mipmap consumption can be confirmed, whether explicit interpolation can be confirmed, what return values or raw diagnostics were retained, and whether the blocker is missing input, a broken reference chain, or the CI queue.

If abnormal behavior appears only in the debug entry point, list that separately rather than folding it into the results for the normal path. DDS and interpolation can be pursued separately in different rounds, with no requirement to reach a joint attribution in the same round. Missing Texture Dimensions is an adjacent issue, see DOC-23; results there cannot replace confirmation here of the consumption state or the interpolation trigger.

Old record
Issue name / call name

Near the resources for MainWindow.xaml.cs

After migration
Callers still using size information

Actual version + entry location + result of this check

Main window entry used only for historical comparison

# Spine Texture State Decision Record

For the 2024.6 compatibility train, keep Spine Texture Status as a compatibility issue rather than concluding that the sprite model has or has not handled it. The existing investigation starts at `UndertaleModLib/Models/UndertaleSprite.cs`; this entry point is useful for revisiting the model's neighboring elements and earlier assessments, but is not enough on its own to establish whether the state difference arises during reading, saving, or display.

The initial draft compared two approaches. The first was to classify the reported state difference directly as a general texture compatibility issue. This would keep the scope of changes small, but would lose the Spine-specific scope. The second was to retain the state name, add notes around a reproducible sample, and then decide whether the model needs to change. The second approach was chosen.

This choice was not made because model files are unimportant, but because no material available at the time could tie the sample results to specific objects in the model. Assuming up front that the problem lies in fields, construction, or conversion branches could easily turn later reading into a search only for material that supports that assessment. Preserving the sample first lets later assessments revisit the same behavior and helps avoid conflating the presence of a resource with a correct result.

Retain a sample that exhibits the difference, the failure text or output bytes captured at the time, and its connection to `UndertaleSprite.cs` for verification. Both failure text and output bytes can serve as material for later comparisons; the former is useful for preserving a readable record of a failure, while the latter is useful for pinning down results that cannot be distinguished through text. They are not a fixed pair of artifacts that must be collected together.

This decision does not require immediately expanding the scope to all sprite paths. A resource being able to find a texture does not mean the reported state difference has disappeared; conversely, different output bytes alone cannot identify saving as the stage where the difference occurs. The sample first bounds the problem; code reading then determines which relationships are worth pursuing further.

No decision has been made on which object should hold the state, or on whether a new conversion branch is needed. At the next review, first confirm the sample's result in the current version, then return to the model path to check the relevant declarations and adjacent processing. If later samples show only general texture differences, separate them from the Spine-specific scope discussed in this record.
